description: We are SpaceCowboys, a small team building MarsPath: a Marswalk planning map of Jezero Crater on real NASA terrain. Our interests are planetary mapping, route planning and honest data visualisation. Skills we welcome: web development (React, TypeScript), Python and GIS, planetary science, and video or design for the demo.
summary:
MarsPath is an interactive map that helps an astronaut plan a walk on Mars. You pick a start and a destination in Jezero Crater, and it compares three walking routes: the shortest, the fastest and the one that costs the least energy. Each route shows distance, walking time, energy, ascent and steepness.

Routes are computed on real 20-metre NASA/USGS terrain from Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter stereo images, using a published model of how fast a suited astronaut walks on slopes and how much energy it takes, at Mars gravity. Ground that is too steep is treated as an obstacle and shown on the map.

The map layers data from four missions: optical imagery (HiRISE, CTX, Viking), thermal infrared (THEMIS), topography and geology, plus the real track and positions of the Perseverance rover as science stops.

It matters because the straight line is rarely the best walk: on our demo route the least-energy path is 34 m longer but 44 minutes faster.
details:
What it does

MarsPath is a web map for planning a walk (EVA) in Jezero Crater. The user picks two points, or uses science stops where the Perseverance rover actually stood, and compares three routes for a suited astronaut: shortest, fastest and least energy. Each route reports distance, walking time, metabolic energy, ascent, the steepest step and how much of the route is steeper than 10 degrees, with an elevation profile and a plain-language explanation of how it differs from the shortest route.

How it works

The backend runs an A* search on the USGS 20 m CTX digital terrain model of Jezero (2.4 million cells). Walking speed by slope and metabolic rate come from published research on EVA traverse planning (Santee et al. 2001; Johnson et al. 2010), applied at Mars gravity. Terrain at or above a user-chosen slope limit is an obstacle. The user can change the crew-plus-suit mass and the slope limit. The frontend draws NASA Mars Trek layers in a Mars coordinate system: HiRISE, CTX and Viking imagery, THEMIS thermal infrared, a geologic map and the rover's track.

Benefits and impact

It shows a crew, a student or a mission planner why the straight line is not the best walk, and what a route costs in time and effort. On our demo route from the landing site to the delta top, the least-energy route is 34 m longer than the shortest but 44 minutes faster.

What we considered

Honesty about the data. A 20 m grid cannot see boulders, and time and energy are model estimates extrapolated from Earth and Apollo-era data, not measurements. The app says so on screen. We checked terrain heights against NASA rover positions, and the routing is covered by automated tests, including comparison with an independent search.

Tools

Python, FastAPI, NumPy, Rasterio; React, TypeScript, MapLibre GL JS, Vite, Tailwind CSS.
